diagnostic_evidence.quote: The method is proven to be unconditionally stable and preserves both mass and energy invariants at the final time.
Let Assumption~\ref{assu:34} be satisfied. Then, for all~$p \in \N$ and~$\rho \in \R$, the family of matrices~$\{\K_n^p(\rho)\}_n$ defined in~\eqref{eq:21} is weakly well-conditioned.
Assume that, for all $p \in \N$ with $p \ge 1$, $h>0$, and $\mu_w > 0$ the variational formulation~\eqref{eq:30} admits a unique solution.

issues.failure_explanation: The abstract, the novelty list and the conclusions state that the method (and the wave-equation method of Section 4) is /proven/ unconditionally stable. What is actually established is conditional: Theorem th:313 presupposes Assumption assu:34 (unique solvability of (10) for all p, h, mu), which is verified only for p=1 and is explicitly left unproved for p>1, and Theorem th:42 likewise presupposes the unproved unique solvability of (30). For p>1 even existence/uniqueness of the discrete solution is conjectural, so the advertised unconditional stability is not proved.

failure_location.quote: demonstrating that it preserves both mass and energy at the final time, and it is unconditionally stable.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Qualify the abstract, novelty and conclusion claims: unconditional stability (weakly well-conditioning) is proved under Assumption 3.4 (resp. the unique-solvability hypothesis of Theorem 4.2), which is established only for p=1.
issues.overall_effect: The advertised scope and guarantee type are overstated: for degrees p>1 the stability statement is conditional on an unverified conjecture, and the same holds for the claimed purely theoretical stability proof for the wave-equation method.
issues.title: Summary overclaims proven unconditional stability
issues.why_classification: Only the summary statements need qualification; every formal result, rate and guarantee survives unchanged, so no mathematical content is lost and no new argument is needed.

issues.failure_explanation: With the stated test function, (14) shows that (\partial_t\psi, w)_{J_T} = \int_0^T|\partial_s\psi|^2e^{-s/T}\,ds is a nonnegative real number, so Re(i(\partial_t\psi, w)) = 0; the displayed identity instead assigns it the value \int_0^T|\partial_s\psi|^2e^{-s/T}\,ds. No choice of conjugation convention repairs this (the second term of the same display is the real part of (\psi,w)), so the inference 'from which we deduce psi = 0' does not follow from the computation as written.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Correct the real part: Re(i(\partial_t\psi, w)) = 0, so the remaining identity mu( (1/(2T))\int_0^T|\psi|^2e^{-s/T} + (1/(2e))|\psi(T)|^2 ) = 0 forces psi = 0 whenever mu != 0; the case mu = 0 is disposed of by testing (13) with w = psi.
issues.overall_effect: The uniqueness half of Proposition 3.2 is unproved as written (existence is fine via the explicit formula); no later result relies on Proposition 3.2.
issues.title: Invalid real-part computation in the uniqueness proof of Proposition 3.2
issues.why_classification: The claim is true and is recovered by deleting one wrong term and adding a one-line degenerate case; the method, statement and scope all survive with a short local repair.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: If $|\mu| < \pi/T$, then problem \eqref{eq:10} has a unique solution.

issues.failure_explanation: The real part of (17) is mu( |\psi_h^p(T)|^2 - Re(\partial_t\psi_h^p,\psi_h^p)_{J_T} ) = 0, so the asserted equality |\psi_h^p(T)|^2 = Re(\partial_t\psi_h^p,\psi_h^p) is obtained by dividing by mu. The stated range |mu| < pi/T includes mu = 0, where this step is invalid and psi_h^p(T) = 0 is not established; the subsequent Poincare step (which needs both endpoint values) therefore does not apply.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Split off mu = 0 before dividing: for mu = 0 the imaginary part of (17) gives ||\partial_t\psi_h^p||_{L^2(0,T)} = 0 directly, whence \psi_h^p = 0.
issues.overall_effect: The uniqueness claim of Proposition 3.3 is unsupported at mu = 0, which lies in its stated parameter range.
issues.title: Degenerate case mu = 0 not covered in the proof of Proposition 3.3
issues.why_classification: A one-line degenerate-case addition completes the case split; the statement, range and conclusion are all preserved.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: In the next proposition, we show that $q^{\K^p(\rho)}$ is a \textit{reciprocal} polynomial, meaning that if $\xi \in \mathbb{C}$ is a root of $q^{\K^p(\rho)}$, then $\xi^{-1}$ is also a root.

issues.failure_explanation: The proof's own display shows that q^{C^p} is anti-palindromic (coefficients c_0,...,-c_0 with c_0 != 0) while q^{B^p} is palindromic; the xi -> xi^{-1} root pairing is not inherited by the combination appearing in the symbol. Already for p=1, Proposition 3.11 gives q^{B^1}(z) = -(z-1)^2 and q^{C^1}(z) = (1/2)(z^2-1), so the symbol of (21) is q^{K^1(rho)}(z) = (z-1)[(-i-rho/2)z + (i-rho/2)], whose roots are 1 and z_2 = (i-rho/2)/(i+rho/2); for rho != 0 one has |z_2| = 1 but z_2^{-1} = conjugate(z_2) != z_2 is not a root. The same failure occurs with the expression printed in (25) (which is itself inconsistent with (21): it omits the factor i and the sign). Consequently the deduction that q^{K^p(rho)} is of type (l, 2p-2l, l), and hence the use of Theorem 3.8 with l = p-1, is invalid.

failure_location.quote: In particular, from these expressions, both~$q^{\B^p}$ and~$q^{\bC^p}$ are reciprocal polynomials, and from \eqref{eq:25}, it follows that~$q^{\K^p(\rho)}$ is also a reciprocal polynomial

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace the reciprocity argument with the correct conjugate-reciprocal (self-inversive) property of the symbol of (21), z^{2p} conjugate(q^{K^p(rho)}(1/conjugate(z))) = -q^{K^p(rho)}(z), which yields the root pairing xi <-> 1/conjugate(xi) and hence equal counts inside and outside the unit circle (type (l, 2p-2l, l)); alternatively obtain the type from a winding-number count or by continuation in rho from rho = 0.
issues.overall_effect: The zero-type classification that drives the weakly well-conditioning conclusion is unproved, so the main stability theorem th:313 and the stability transfer for the wave-equation method th:42 lose their proof; the numerical conclusions built on them are unaffected.
issues.title: Symbol polynomial is not reciprocal as claimed; zero type of q^K unproved
issues.why_classification: A load-bearing structural claim of the main proof is false and must be replaced by a different root-pairing/zero-count argument; the repair is contained and keeps every statement and guarantee, but it is a replacement argument rather than a local edit.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: For~$\rho>0$ and~$p \in \mathbb{N}$, the function $K_p(\theta,\rho)$ has exactly 2 simple zeros
of $\K_n^p(\rho)$ are nonzero for all $\rho>0$ and $p \in \N$

issues.failure_explanation: Every step of the chain supports only rho > 0: the non-vanishing of the outer codiagonals is invoked for rho > 0, and Proposition 3.12 (two simple zeros of K_p on [-pi,pi]) is stated for rho > 0 and its proof uses partial_theta K_p(0,rho) = -rho != 0, which fails at rho = 0, where theta = 0 is a double zero and Lemma 3.10 does not give two simple zeros. No stated result covers rho < 0, yet the theorem claims rho in R, which is needed because the discrete eigenvalues mu of the Hamiltonian range over all of R.

failure_location.quote: Then, for all~$p \in \N$ and~$\rho \in \R$, the family of matrices~$\{\K_n^p(\rho)\}_n$ defined in~\eqref{eq:21} is weakly well-conditioned.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Restate and prove Proposition 3.12 for rho != 0 (its argument only uses rho != 0) and dispose of rho = 0 separately, e.g. via K^p_n(0) = i B^p_n whose weakly well-conditioning is cited, or by counting the double zero z = 1 of q^{K^p(0)} with multiplicity.
issues.overall_effect: The unconditional-stability statement of th:313 is unsupported for non-positive rho = mu*h, a regime required by the intended application; th:42 only uses rho > 0 and is unaffected.
issues.title: Theorem 3.13 quantifies over all rho although the analysis covers only rho > 0
issues.why_classification: The extension is a local statement change plus a one-line degenerate case; the conclusion, its type and the advertised scope all survive.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: \textbf{Compute} the complex Schur decomposition $(\mathbf{Q}_{h_t}^p,\mathbf{R}_{h_t}^p)$ of $(\mi \B_{h_t}^p)^{-1} \bC_{h_t}^p$, and compute $(\mathbf{R}_{h_t}^p)^{-1}$

issues.failure_explanation: Composing the five steps with G = (iB)^{-1}C = Q R Q^H gives Psi = -[G (x) A + G^{-1} (x) M]^{-1} (B^{-1} (x) I) F, whereas (35) requires Psi = [iB (x) M + C (x) A]^{-1} F. Matching the M-blocks would force G^{-1} = -i I, which is impossible for general data. Concretely, for scalar data B = b, C = c, M = m, A = a the algorithm returns Psi = i c F/(b^2 m - c^2 a) while (35) gives Psi = F/(i b m + c a); e.g. b = c = m = a = 1 gives Psi = 0 from the algorithm and Psi = F/(1+i) from the system. The step-4 matrix and the scaling/sign of the right-hand side and of the final output are mutually inconsistent (a correct Schur solver would use e.g. R (x) A + I (x) M with right-hand side -i Y and no final sign flip, or equivalently I (x) A + R^{-1} (x) M with a correspondingly transformed unknown).
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Re-derive the Schur-based solver and correct the steps, e.g.: with (iB)^{-1}C = Q R Q^H solve ((iB) (x) I) Y = F, set Y <- (Q^H (x) I) Y, solve (R (x) A + I (x) M) Z = Y and return Psi = (Q (x) I) Z.
issues.overall_effect: The solver specified in Section 5.1 does not compute the solution of the discrete system; the structural claims (independent small solves in step 2, matrix-vector products in steps 3 and 5, block upper triangular step 4) hold only for a corrected algorithm.
issues.title: Algorithm 1 does not solve the discrete system (35)
issues.why_classification: The input-output contract of the algorithm fails outright and no single forced correction exists (the matrix, the factor i and the final sign must all be re-derived), but the corrected algorithm keeps the same Schur/triangular structure and cost, so no global architecture or complexity guarantee is lost.
